paras: The killing of L. A. Planving was the ambush shooting of La Forest A. Planving, a Black minister and principal of the Pointe Coupee Industrial College, near Oscar, Louisiana, on a Sunday night at the end of August 1903. No arrest was reported, and accounts of who fired the shots differed. White dispatches tied the killing to his alleged "incendiary speeches," a charge the Black press and the American Missionary Association (AMA) rejected.

According to a New Orleans dispatch, Planving, a Straight University graduate and former New Orleans pastor, had raised money among white and Black residents of Pointe Coupee Parish to start an industrial school modeled on Tuskegee, with four assistants and 150 pupils. Booker T. Washington was to have visited the area the following month as his guest to lecture. That dispatch said "the best of relations" had always existed in the parish, and the AMA's Rev. C. J. Ryder said Planving had written two weeks earlier of getting along well with whites. A later report in The Sun, however, said three shots had been fired into his house two weeks before.

According to a Memphis Commercial Appeal special from New Roads, Planving was riding home on the main road near False River when he was fired upon from a cotton field. The first shot struck his horse and the second struck him in the back of the head, killing him instantly. A shorter dispatch put the shooting at about seven o'clock near Oscar, four miles from New Roads, by "unknown parties."

No report of an arrest, inquest or trial was found, and the St. Louis Palladium's dispatch said the shooters were said to be known, "but nothing has been done to them." Ryder, the AMA's corresponding secretary, said he would write Governor Heard that the association expected those responsible to be "promptly dealt with," and in October the AMA passed resolutions complimenting Heard for his stand, which the report did not describe. At the same meeting Rev. P. S. Moxom made the killing the occasion of a sermon on the race problem. A New Orleans dispatch predicted that Black residents believed to have helped Planving "in disorganizing labor" would be ordered out of the parish; no later report of expulsions was found.

Most white papers ran the Commercial Appeal special on September 2, among them the New Haven Journal and Courier, the Savannah Morning News and the Indianapolis Journal. It said "it is claimed" that Planving had advised Black people not to work for whites and that "it is believed" these "alleged utterances" had much to do with the killing. The Portland Daily Press ran a New Orleans dispatch, under "RACE HATRED MURDER," that blamed him for racial bitterness and a labor shortage, while the Southern Sentinel of Winnfield, Louisiana, gave the killing one line. In New England, the Springfield Weekly Republican carried the AMA's denial and the Worcester Spy reprinted a Hartford Times editorial calling the murder "an omen of what is coming."

The Black press called it murder by whites. The Cleveland Gazette headlined "AN EDUCATOR MURDERED" with the deck "Killed by White Brutes Because of a Remark" and answered the white account with "All of which are LIES." A Gazette editorial compared the case to the driving out of Rev. Byron Gunner and argued it showed why Washington could not lead the race. The Palladium's dispatch named "Prominent white residents" as the ambushers, and later items in the Chicago Broad Ax and the Seattle Republican tied the killing to Southern hostility to Black schooling and economic independence.

Against the wire's "unknown persons" and the Black press's white ambushers, a New Orleans dispatch in The Sun said it was "understood" the killer was a Black man who said he had been paid, without saying by whom. Most reports gave the day as Sunday night, but the Portland Daily Press said Saturday and the Seattle Republican "last Monday."

reader.title: Killing of L. A. Planving
bases: Planving was shot dead from ambush by men hidden in a cotton field, a killing the white wire tied to his alleged speeches against working for whites and the Black press and a Hartford editorial attributed to local white men (A8, A27, A29); one New Orleans report instead names a hired Black killer (A13), so this is classed as a lynching-type assassination with doubt about the group.

He was shot dead from ambush (A8, A2), and reports attribute the killing to a decision by local whites angered by his alleged speeches (A26, A27, A29), a racial pretext; but no report counts the attackers beyond 'parties' or 'persons' and one says a single paid Black man fired (A13), so the three-or-more element is unclear.

The ambush killing near Oscar is reported independently by the New Orleans dispatch to The Sun (A1), the AP New Roads item (A2), the Commercial Appeal special (A8) and the Palladium's New Roads dispatch (A27); who fired and why remain disputed (A13, A27).

accounts.label: Commercial Appeal special (white wire)
accounts.gist: Unknown persons fired from a cotton field as he rode home; it was claimed he had made incendiary speeches against working for whites, and these 'alleged utterances' were believed to have caused the killing.

accounts.label: New Orleans dispatch on race feeling
accounts.gist: Racial bitterness had arisen since Planving came, whites held him responsible, labor had become hard to get, and Black residents who helped him might be ordered out.

accounts.label: New Orleans 'hired killer' report
accounts.gist: It was 'understood' the killer was a Black man who said he was paid; an earlier attempt had fired three shots into his house.

accounts.label: Black press
accounts.gist: White men ambushed and murdered him because his school work was too successful; the speech charge was 'LIES'; the shooters were said to be known but untouched.

accounts.label: American Missionary Association
accounts.gist: His employers said the incendiary charge was at variance with his character and pressed the governor for prompt action.

framing.detail: Most white papers ran the Commercial Appeal special under headlines such as 'ASSASSINATION OF A NEGRO' and 'A NEGRO PREACHER SHOT FROM AMBUSH', repeating the 'incendiary speeches' claim as hearsay ('it is claimed').
The Portland Daily Press dispatch 'RACE HATRED MURDER' presented whites' grievances against Planving (racial bitterness, labor shortage) and the likely expulsion of his supporters without challenge.
Northern Congregational and New England papers carried the AMA's denial and a Hartford Times editorial calling the murder 'an omen of what is coming'.

The Cleveland Gazette headlined 'AN EDUCATOR MURDERED... Killed by White Brutes' and called the white account lies; later editorials used the case against Washington's accommodationism and Southern hostility to Black schools.
